title: Every step reads what the person asked
description:
Repository: JKershaw/LinearViewer (Harbour).

**What this is for.** Harbour passes a ticket from step to step, and each step mostly reads the one before it. The plan reads the brief. Review checks the build against the plan. Close-out reads review's summary. Then close-out's tidy of the description removes the plan, and the reasons behind it go too. Each hand-off keeps the detail and loses a little of what the person wanted, like a photocopy of a photocopy. On 1 November a request for "a full guide" became a thin one at the first hand-off, and review approved it because it matched the plan (on main: `docs/papers/harbour/one-feature-twice.md`).

**What we want.** The person's own words are the fixed point that every step reads directly. What they wrote when they asked stays on the ticket as written, and no step rewrites or prunes it. The plan, review and close-out each judge the work against it, as well as against the step before. Where a step narrows what was asked, it says so openly, or asks, rather than letting it happen quietly. We decided on 7 November not to add a step that rewrites or summarises the person's words: that would be one more copy.

Most of this should come out of the prompts rather than go in, leaving the stages shorter and plainer.

**Appetite:** err larger. If the cleanest way to get here is to change how the description is shaped, or what close-out prunes, do it.

**Done looks like:** on any finished ticket, the person's original words are still there, and each judging step's verdict says how the work met them. The pull request says which hand-offs changed and which were left alone, and why.

## Implementation Plan

*Attempt 2, upstream. Planned at* `93a37ab6` *(main), with PR #2348 open at* `e8ef01b1`*. This replaces revision 2 of the plan. Pieces A–C (LIN-4351–4353, PRs #2345–2347) built that plan in full, and it stays readable in this task's snapshots and in PR #2347's hand-off table. Sources: John's ruling* `lin4345-per-sentence-outcome` *(18:03, recorded in the 18:04 comment), the per-sentence replay (*`docs/reviews/lin-4345-per-sentence-replay-2026-11-07.md` *on #2348), the A/B record (*`docs/reviews/lin-4085-ab-run-2026-11-01.md`*) and LIN-4085's task snapshots. Each was checked against the code at that sha.*

### What this is for, and what done looks like

The person's words now reach every step intact. That was A–C's job, and it is done. What still fails is the cut itself. On LIN-4085, scoping turned "essentially a full guide on how to properly configure Harper for whatever your situation is" into "the guide's job is to sequence the human's few clicks". It also put the guide under the frozen prompt-size rule (In Scope item 5, snapshot `2026-11-01T17:39:57Z`), and the plan then set a cap of about 4.5 KB. Neither stage said it was cutting anything. In the replays, all six reviews approved the 577-word guide, even the three that quoted the sentence whole. LIN-1596's cut was different: scoping wrote it down under "Out of scope — split out", and all six reviews caught it.

So the miss happens at the stage that makes the cut, not at the stage that judges it. John's ruling sends the next attempt there: scoping and plan name each cut to the ask and route it to a ruling.

**Done when** (John's words, kept open by `merge-carry` and `keep-upstream`): "If LIN-4085's request for 'a full guide' were replayed through this change, its review would judge against those words, not against the plan." The evidence John asked for at 18:03 is a replay of LIN-4085's scoping and plan, with several runs per arm. A run passes when scoping or plan names the reduction of "full guide" as a cut and raises a ruling. This plan adds one link of its own, marked as such: review runs on a plan that names the cut, to show the chain reaches review's verdict.

The ask has not drifted. The done-when is the same; this attempt goes after it at an earlier stage.

### The cause, at HEAD

Two lines tell the deciding stages that cutting the ask is their own call:

1. `STAGE_LEADS.scoping` (`lib/prompt-template-defs.js:84`): "What is in and out of scope is yours to decide; read the code first, and flag for the human only product or intent questions."
2. `DECIDE` (`lib/prompts/stage-intent.js:6`) is appended as Scope and Authority to research, scoping, design, spike, plan, breakdown, implementation and blocked. It says "Engineering choices … are yours" and "Only a change the team would need to hear about before it happens goes to the human". A size cap or a reframing assumption reads as an engineering choice.

Nothing says that a reduction made through an assumption, a design choice or a budget is a cut to the ask. Scoping's write-up format also has no place for one. LIN-4085's cuts went under Assumptions (`:595`) and into In Scope, while Out of Scope (`:594`) is defined as "different problems".

### The change

1. **One rule, in one home: the** `DECIDE` **line in** `stage-intent.js`**.** It gains one sentence, a `CUT` constant used only in `DECIDE`. The builder may tighten the wording but must keep all three parts:
   * Any sentence or clause of the `## As asked` block that the work will not deliver in full is a cut, whatever made it: a scope call, an assumption, a design choice, a budget or size limit, or moving it to another ticket.
   * Each cut is written where the stage writes, quoting the words it reduces.
   * The cuts go to the person as **one** ruling, through the existing route (the closing contract's `DECISION:` line, `docs/runner-prompt.md:166-170`, which allows one per finish). Until the person answers, a cut is not agreed.

   Draft: "Reducing the `## As asked` block is not yours: any sentence or clause the work will not deliver in full, by a scope call, an assumption, a design choice, a budget or another ticket, is a cut. Name each where you write, quoting the words it reduces, and raise them as one ruling; unanswered, a cut is not agreed."

   **Why this home.** `DECIDE` is the line that says what each deciding stage owns, so the rule reaches every place a cut can be made without a copy per template. Design and research can choose a smaller shape, breakdown can drop a slice, and implementation can write less than planned.

   **Why not** `ASK`**.** `ASK` is shared with the judging stages and close-out. Review and plan-review already have their own narrowing rules, including review's per-sentence wording, which John keeps. A second copy there is exactly what LIN-4350 and LIN-4354 are removing.
2. **Scoping's lead loses the licence.** Delete "What is in and out of scope is yours to decide; … flag for the human only product or intent questions." and keep "read the code first". The router quotes only the first sentence of a lead (`lib/prompt-templates.js:440`), so the routing prompt does not change.
3. **Scoping's write-up gets a place for cuts.** The Out of Scope bullet (`:594`) also holds each cut to the ask, quoted, with its ruling. Draft: "Out of Scope: different problems excluded, and each cut to the ask, quoted, with its ruling; the cause of this one is never out of scope." Reviews reliably catch a cut that is written down.
4. **Plan's opening paragraph** (`:255`). This is LIN-4021's agreed text, and its clause about the asker is the only part touched. The plan opens with the problem as the block puts it and what done looks like. It then lists each cut to the block, quoted, with its ruling, or says there is none. That includes cuts it inherits from scoping or research. Requiring "none" makes the plan answer the question rather than skip it.
5. **Completion signals** (`lib/completion-signals.js`: scoping at :109, plan at :54). Each gets one matching signal: cuts quoted with their ruling, or none. These signals reach the prompts page, the audit and `formatSignalsForPrompt`. C kept review's and plan-review's signals in step with their templates the same way.
6. **Docs.** Add one sentence to the As-asked paragraph of `docs/architecture/prompt-system.md`: deciding stages name cuts and raise one ruling, and the rule lives in `stage-intent.js`.

**Not changing:**

* **No new format code reads**, such as a `Cuts:` line in `lib/prompt-contract.js`. Code already records rulings, and review catches a cut that is written down. A format would add a reader and a contract row with no demonstrated need. Revisit it only if the replay shows plans leaving the cut list out.
* **No new parking rule.** A stage that raises the ruling ends `BLOCKED` with its `DECISION:`, as it does today. What follows is up to the orchestrator and the person: LIN-4085's run went on while scoping's ruling was open. If the person rejects the cut, review's Needs Discussion holds the merge.

**Alternatives set aside:**

* **A third change to review's wording.** Two replays showed that review judges sufficiency the same way whatever it is told, and John chose upstream.
* **Per-sentence accounting in scoping and plan, like review's.** That makes stages quote the ask, and quoting has already failed to change judgement. Asking a stage for the reductions it made itself, such as a cap it set or an assumption it wrote, asks for something that stage actually knows.
* **The rule in the scoping and plan templates only.** Design, research, breakdown and implementation can cut too, and two copies drift apart.
* **Code that detects cuts.** Whether "few clicks" narrows "a full guide" is a judgement, not something code can match.

### Hand-offs: changed and left alone

| Hand-off | Change |
| -- | -- |
| scoping | the lead loses "yours to decide"; Out of Scope holds cuts, quoted, with their ruling |
| plan | the opening lists cuts, quoted, with their ruling, or says there are none |
| research, design, spike, breakdown, implementation, blocked | inherit the rule through `DECIDE`; no text of their own |
| **left alone:** plan-review | agreed wording; it already sends "what should the task deliver" to Needs Discussion and names narrowing in its verdict, and it now reads a cut that is written down |
| **left alone:** review | John keeps the per-sentence wording (#2348) |
| **left alone:** close-out | has its own `ASK` line, and an inside item can never be filed away |
| **left alone:** bug | a judging stage that proposes a fix against the cause; review's per-sentence check covers it |
| **left alone:** triage, the reading passes, the Survey | none of them decides what gets built |
| **left alone:** the brief | it already flags departures under Open questions |
| **left alone:** a subtask's quoted parent ask | the rule names the stage's own block; breakdown is already told to keep the task's intent |

### Every place, and how we know

The behaviour: **a stage that decides what gets built reduces what the** `## As asked` **block asks for, without naming the reduction as a cut and raising it.**

* **A search anyone can repeat:** `grep -rn "are yours\|yours to\|in and out of scope\|what is left out\|Out of Scope" lib/prompts/*.js lib/prompt-template-defs.js lib/prompt-formatters.js lib/proxy-preamble.js lib/brief.js`. At `93a37ab6` it finds:
  * `DECIDE` and close-out's line (`stage-intent.js:6`, `:29`);
  * the scoping lead (`:84`) and scoping's Out of Scope bullet (`:594`);
  * plan's "what is left out" (`:263`);
  * the blocked, triage and breakdown leads (`:77`, `:81`, `:82`);
  * five lines in `lib/prompts/autopilot-kickoff.js` (`:362`–`:557`).
* **In scope:** `:6`, `:84`, `:594`, and plan's opening at `:255`, which `grep -n "As asked" lib/prompt-template-defs.js` finds.
* **Out, each with its reason:**
  * close-out (`:29`): see the table above.
  * `:263`: LIN-4021's agreed text, and not about the asker. The `DECIDE` rule now governs any part of the ask that is left out.
  * the blocked, triage and breakdown leads: they grant authority over obstacles, ticket fields and the shape of subtasks, not over the ask.
  * autopilot-kickoff: those lines are about the orchestrator's seat (dispatch and merges), not the ask.
* **Pins on the old wording:** `grep -rln "Engineering choices, fixing at the cause\|What is in and out of scope\|Different problems excluded\|It opens with the problem as the" tests docs scripts` finds only two files:
  * `tests/judge/audit-report.fixture.json`: update it deliberately if `tests/judge/replay.spec.js` compares it with live text;
  * a historical evidence note, which stays as it is.
* **What catches the rest:** witness 1 asserts that the rule has one home across every rendered stage. A new deciding stage inherits the rule by being `DECIDE`, and a copy anywhere else fails the test.

### Witnesses

1. **One home (unit test, fails before the change).** Every stage whose `STAGE_INTENT` includes `DECIDE` renders the cut rule exactly once. No judging, reading or filing stage renders it.
2. **The routing prompt is unchanged.** `tests/unit/stage-router-prompt-snapshots.test.js` and `scripts/eval/meta-prompt.baseline.txt` pass without an edit.
3. **Budget.** `tests/unit/prompt-size-budget.test.js` passes. The ceilings for `stage-intent.js` source and the eight `DECIDE` stages' rendered prompts rise only with the reason recorded beside them, net of the scoping deletion. Prefer cuts wherever they are found. `FROZEN_TOTAL_BYTES` moves by the exact sum.
4. **The replay.** This is the behavioural witness. It is evidence for review, not a CI test. It reuses #2348's harness (`docs/reviews/_evidence-2026-11-07-lin4345-replay/build_tickets.py` and `render.mjs`), rendering `generatePrompt('scoping' | 'plan', …)`.
   * **Inputs.** Two LIN-4085 task snapshots:
     * `2026-11-01T17:35:35.250Z`, before scoping: the filed request and triage's comment;
     * `2026-11-01T17:39:57.470Z`, before plan: scoping's output with "few clicks" and the size guard, and three comments.

     The filed request is sealed into an As-asked block the way `build_tickets.py` does it. The code is a clone at `e1f75fe7`, where both runs started, with no later history.
   * **Arms.** Old is `main` after #2348; new is the branch.
     * Scoping: 3 runs per arm on the 17:35 snapshot.
     * Plan: 3 runs per arm on the 17:39 snapshot. Both arms read the same old scoping text, so the difference isolates plan's wording.
   * **Each run** is a fresh subagent with no tracker and no network. It writes the description section it would write, and any `DECISION:` it would raise, to a file in its run directory. Every run gets the same brief, which names neither the guide nor cuts.
   * **Pass per run** (John's criterion, recorded before any run): the output names a reduction of "essentially a full guide on how to properly configure Harper for whatever your situation is" as a cut, and raises a ruling for it. Naming it can mean quoting the sentence or naming the guide's reduction: the few-clicks framing or a size cap.
     * It **fails** if it reduces the sentence without naming the cut, treats the cut as agreed or as the stage's own call, or names it without raising a ruling.
     * An output that keeps the sentence in full, with no cap and no reduction, leaves nothing to name. It is recorded separately, as neither pass nor fail. That category is this plan's own addition.
   * **Reading an effect** follows #2348's pre-registration: only a clean separation counts, meaning new 3/3 and old 0/3 on at least one of the two stages. The record predicts old 0/3 on both.
   * **Review link** (this plan's own; it closes the chain the done-when describes). Three runs of review at #2348's wording on the LIN-4085 review inputs from #2348's replay (snapshot `18:19:44`, code `4f247b68`), with the description's plan section replaced by a new-arm plan output that named the cut, its ruling unanswered. A run passes on Needs Discussion, or when it names the cut as unagreed. Run this only if the plan arm passes.
   * **Over-asking control.** Three runs of the new plan arm on one ticket whose delivered work met its filed ask in full. The ticket and the reason for choosing it are named in the pre-registration before any run. A good candidate is one whose review approved with no narrowing and whose person accepted the result. A run passes when it raises no cut ruling that the scorer cannot tie to a real reduction of a sentence in the block. Also record, for every run in every arm, how many cut rulings it raises.
   * **Order.** Commit the change-log row (`scripts/prompt-template-change-log.md`, expected direction `down`) and the pre-registration before any run starts. The results go in `docs/reviews/lin-4345-upstream-cut-replay-<date>.md`, with the evidence folder beside it. There are 18 runs in all.

### Likeliest ways this breaks

1. **A flood of rulings.** Stages raise a cut for every small choice, spending the person's attention (Principle 0). Raising all cuts as one ruling limits this, and the control and the per-run count measure it. If the control fails, tighten the definition ("a sentence or clause not delivered") rather than adding exceptions.
2. **The stage still does not see its own reduction as a cut.** It reads "few clicks" as a way of framing the guide, not as a cut. The plan arm, fed the old scoping text, tests whether plan catches a cut it inherits. If both arms fail, record the done-when as unmet, say what the outputs show, and do not add more text.
3. **The budget fights back.** The rule lands in eight rendered prompts. Pay for it with the scoping deletion and with other cuts found along the way; any raise carries its reason (LIN-3633).
4. **LIN-4021's wording drifts.** Plan's template changes beyond the asker clause. The witness is a diff of the plan template limited to its opening paragraph, and the change-log row says so.

### Constraints from recent history (`git log --oneline -15` on these files)

* **LIN-4021** (`8f6690f2`): the plan and plan-review bodies are agreed wording. Change only the clauses about the asker.
* **LIN-3203, LIN-3633:** prompt size is frozen. A ceiling rises only with its reason recorded beside it, and `FROZEN_TOTAL_BYTES` moves by the exact sum.
* **LIN-1661:** the change-log row goes in before any result is read.
* **LIN-4353** (`cdc324bc`): plan's opening clause is C's wording. Keep its pointer to the block, and do not inline the ask (#369).
* **PR #2348** (`e8ef01b1`, open) changes review's lines in `prompt-template-defs.js`, the budget test, the change log and review's completion signal. Build on `main` after it merges; ruling `lin4354-pr2348-order` already puts it first. If it has not merged, branch from its head and rebase onto `main` once it does.
* **Other tickets in flight:**
  * LIN-4354's pieces (LIN-4360 / PR #2350, LIN-4362) rebase onto #2348. They touch the block's code, the contract's reader table and the docs, but not `stage-intent.js` or the scoping and plan text.
  * LIN-4350 folds rules together after this lands.
  * LIN-4348 waits on this.

### Session fit

This **fits one session**. The prompt edits touch three files; then come the pins, the budget, one sentence of docs, and the replay with the harness #2348 already built. The last implementation pass built a wording change and ran 12 replays in a single session.

plan-review due: no. One session is enough. The change adds a rule rather than loosening a validation, guard or contract. It adds no new format and touches no credentials, merge rules or dispatch path. The risk it does carry, over-asking, is what the replay's control measures.

## Survey open-0: LIN-4345 @ e63c2f69d

**The ticket names close-out's prune, but that's the last copy, not the first.** Every dispatch's preamble (`lib/proxy-preamble.js:261-265`) says "Start from the distilled brief … supersedes stale wording; read it before the raw description". `lib/brief.js` tells its model to "Supersede stale original wording … write it as if framed fresh today", with "the description is the seed". So the summarising step that was ruled out on 7 Nov already exists, and every stage reads it first. If the brief is left alone, keeping the original on the ticket won't help much, because judges will still read the copy.

**The description has no boundary around "what the person wrote".** Scoping (`lib/prompt-template-defs.js:579`), research (455), design (623) and plan (226) all write into the description. Close-out then rewrites the whole body with a PATCH (1063). "Never prune the original problem statement" (1064) depends on an agent telling which paragraphs are original after three stages have edited around them. It also cites a scoping "single source of truth" instruction that no longer exists. With prompts alone, that stays guesswork.

**Some of this is already done, and the gap is uneven.** Plan already opens "in the asker's terms" and flags drift. Plan-review already raises Needs Discussion when the disagreement is about what to deliver. Review doesn't do either: it starts by "reading the plan", and its Gap Analysis is "against the plan". That is exactly how LIN-4085 got "the deliverable meets the plan". Close-out's summary then reads review's ledger. So most of the change belongs in review and close-out, while plan and plan-review should mostly lose text rather than gain it.

**Feedback tickets point the other way.** `routes/workspace-api-feedback.js:110` tells autopilot to "Treat the description as a starting hypothesis, not a specification". For a ticket filed from the widget, that description *is* the person's words. Asking the agent to understand them is fine, but calling them a hypothesis invites narrowing.

**"The person's words" isn't always well defined.** Agents file many tickets themselves: close-out follow-ups (FOLLOW_UP_SHAPE), survey offshoots and breakdown children. A breakdown child carries "a copied slice of an approved parent plan". These need a rule for who the asker is, and for whether a child reads its parent's original words.

**Cost.** About 27 unit test files import the templates, and some pin exact phrases (`prompt-templates.test.js`, `proxy-preamble.test.js`, `helpers/frozen-resolvers-6ea1371e.js`). Cutting prose will break tests that check wording rather than behaviour. Budget for that.

**What I'd do first:** decide where the as-filed words live, and how a stage finds them, before editing any prompt. My proposal:
- a fixed block, e.g. `## As asked`, written once when the ticket is filed;
- stages write around it with `appendBlock`/`replace`, never inside it;
- the description PATCH route refuses any body that changes it;
- the brief quotes the block verbatim and never supersedes it.

After that, the prompt work is mostly deletion. Review and close-out each gain one line: judge against *As asked*, and say where the work narrowed it. The cheapest test is the one the essay already proposes: replay LIN-4085's review with the block present.

## Survey global: LIN-4345 @ e63c2f69d

**Where it lands.** `lib/prompt-template-defs.js` (plan :207, plan-review :733, review :860, close-out :988), `lib/prompt-contract.js`, and the brief: `lib/brief.js` and `lib/proxy-preamble.js:260-272`. Tests g1–g6 in `tests/unit/prompt-templates.test.js` pin the prune. The file is improving: net −91 lines since 1 Oct. Half of the ask is already met. Since LIN-4021, plan opens "in the asker's terms" and plan-review judges "against what the person who asked needs". Review still starts "by reading the plan", and close-out reads only review's summary.

**This ticket is aimed at a symptom.** The rewrite-and-summarise step that 7 Nov ruled out already exists, and it sits in front of every stage. The brief's system prompt says "Supersede stale original wording… Be denser and shorter". The preamble tells every agent to read the brief "before the raw description". This ticket's own brief shows the drift: "Most of this should come out of the prompts rather than go in" became "Prefer moving the change into prompts/process rather than adding more ticket content", which says the opposite. If only the plan, review and close-out prompts change, every step still reads the reduced copy first.

There is a second cause. The description is one shared, editable buffer: research, scoping, design and plan all write into it, then close-out rewrites the whole thing with PATCH. Nothing marks which words are the person's. "Never prune: the original problem statement" asks the last stage to tell what was original after four rewrites. That rule also points at scoping's "single source of truth" instruction, which no longer exists. Test g4 still pins the pointer.

**Done the obvious way**, by adding "also check the original ask" to review and close-out, you get a fourth wording of a rule plan and plan-review already state differently and more prompt text. An `## Original request` heading would also have to be taught to:
- `prompt-contract.js` (its CONTRACT_LINES and the table in its header)
- close-out's keep-word-for-word list
- tests g4/g5
- `docs/architecture/prompt-system.md:42`
- the required row in `scripts/prompt-template-change-log.md`

Tests would catch a change to the prune wording. Nothing would catch a brief that keeps paraphrasing, or a stale architecture doc.

**What would leave it better, within this task.** Fix the point by construction, not instruction:
- One block holds the person's words and no stage edits it, stated once as a contract line.
- The prune becomes "nothing above that block's end". That deletes the never-prune list and the dangling pointer.
- Review starts from what was asked, then the plan.
- The brief quotes that block word for word instead of superseding it. That is one constant in `brief.js` and a few preamble lines, and the rest depends on it.

**Better still, but not this task's.** The description is also state that code parses: `## Implementation Plan`, the session-fit phrase and `plan-review due:` are read by `recommendation-facts.js`, `plan-review-round-trips.js`, `file-pointer.js` and `follow-on-ratio.js`. Moving that state out of prose, and asking whether a summarising brief should come before agent work at all, are larger questions.

## Size of the move (the person's call)

Err larger, John's standing answer.

Both Surveys found the cause further up than this ticket says. The distilled brief that every step reads first already rewrites the person's words ("supersede stale original wording"). And the description is one shared space that several stages write into, so nothing marks what the person actually wrote. The Surveys caught that brief step reversing this very ticket: "Most of this should come out of the prompts" became "prefer moving the change into prompts/process".

So the move is larger. Make the person's words something no step can change, through how it's built rather than by asking agents to be careful, and have the brief carry them word for word. With that in place, review and close-out judge against those words. Plan and plan-review, which already say this in their own way, should lose text rather than gain it, and close-out's tidy keeps the words. Some tests pin wording rather than behaviour; where they break, move them to pin behaviour. And because nothing today would notice a brief that kept paraphrasing, leave a check that fails if the person's words reach a step changed.

Whose words count is partly a question of values. Some tickets are filed by agents (follow-ups, breakdown children, Survey offshoots). Tickets filed from feedback are currently told to treat the person's words as "a starting hypothesis". Say in the pull request what you chose for each and why, and raise a ruling where it turns on what John wants rather than on the code.

Once you've done the rest, say whether the distilled brief still earns its place in front of every step. Don't remove it here. If you think it should go, that's a ruling for John.

This runs first in the round. LIN-4348 waits for it, because both change the stage templates and the prompt size budget.

**Done when** no step can alter the person's words, every step reads them as written, and review's verdict says how the work met them. If LIN-4085's request for "a full guide" were replayed through this change, its review would judge against those words, not against the plan.

**John, 7 Nov (~10:20 UTC): he's open to improving the brief endpoint itself.**

The size call said to leave the distilled brief in place and raise a ruling if it should go. You can now go further: improve the brief as part of this move, for the same purpose, so that the person's words reach every step intact and nothing between them and the step thins them out. That includes how it's written and what it runs on. It runs on `openai/gpt-5.4-mini` today, and everything else is now on Opus.

Removing the brief altogether is still John's call. If that's where the work points, raise it as a ruling.

This widens what you may do. It adds nothing to what done means.

## Plan — LIN-4345

The plan is now in the description under `## Implementation Plan`, planned at `e63c2f69`.

**The decision.** The person's words go in a fixed `## As asked` block at the top of the description. The proxy refuses any agent write that changes that block, or that adds one to a ticket without it. Code seals the block when a ticket is filed through Harbour (proxy, session or feedback), or on its first dispatch if it has no earlier dispatch row. Code also puts the block word for word at the top of the brief, so the brief no longer rewrites what was asked. With that in place, review and close-out judge against the block, and close-out prunes only below it (no block means no prune). Plan and plan-review get shorter.

**Sessions:** two. Piece A, the mechanism, lands first; piece B, the prompts and wording, follows it. plan-review due: yes, because the plan needs more than one session, guards the proxy's description write contract, and adds a write on the dispatch path.

**For the PR to rule on:** whose words count for tickets agents file. The recommendation is that the block holds whatever was filed, by whoever filed it.

### Plan Review Verdict

**Verdict:** Request Changes. The approach is right, but two parts of the seal would lock the wrong text into the block, and one of them weakens the plan-review gate.
